tips.title: f(3) is an instruction, not a multiplication
tips.body: $f(3)$ does **not** mean $f \times 3$. It means "put $3$ in wherever $x$ appears". For $f(x) = 3x - 2$, $f(3) = 3 \times 3 - 2 = 7$. The bracket holds the input, exactly like the bracket on a calculator key.

tips.title: In fg(x) the inner one goes first
tips.body: Read $fg(x)$ from the inside out: $g$ acts on $x$, then $f$ acts on the result. It is $f(g(x))$, so $g$ runs first even though $f$ is written first. Nearly every composite function mark lost is lost right here.

tips.title: Find an inverse by rearranging
tips.body: Write $y = f(x)$, swap the letters so it reads $x = f(y)$, then make $y$ the subject. That last step is ordinary rearranging, which you already know. For $f(x) = 3x - 2$: $x = 3y - 2$, so $y = \dfrac{x + 2}{3}$, and that is $f^{-1}(x)$.

tips.title: Test an inverse by undoing
tips.body: An inverse should take you straight back where you started, so $f^{-1}(f(4))$ must be $4$. Pick any number, run it through $f$, run the answer through $f^{-1}$, and see whether you land on what you began with. It takes ten seconds and catches a sign error every time.

why.matters:
A function is a rule with a promise attached: one input, one output, every time. That promise is small and it is what everything else rests on. Because a function is single-valued you can feed it into another and be sure of the result, and because it is a named thing — $f$, not "the rule where you double and add one" — you can talk about it without writing it out.

The two operations that follow are the useful ones. **Composing** is doing one after another, and the order changes the answer. **Inverting** is undoing, which some functions allow and some do not. Between them they cover most of what is done to a number between it being typed in and being shown on a screen.

examples.title: The voucher and the ten per cent
examples.body:
A shop has 10% off and you also hold a £5 voucher. Which comes first? Call the discount $f(x) = 0.9x$ and the voucher $g(x) = x - 5$, and the two orders are two different composites.

On a £50 basket, taking the percentage first costs £40.00 and handing over the voucher first costs £40.50. On £80 it is £67.00 against £67.50. The gap is 50p both times, and the algebra says why. The voucher first is $fg(x) = 0.9(x - 5) = 0.9x - 4.50$; the percentage first is $gf(x) = 0.9x - 5$. The difference is 50p for **every** basket, because it is a constant.

Taking the percentage first is the better order, because the voucher then comes off in full instead of being discounted along with everything else. This is why the terms and conditions specify an order rather than leaving it to the till — $fg$ and $gf$ are different functions, and here the difference is money.

visual.alt: A table of two baskets put through a discount and a voucher in each order, showing the same fifty pence difference on both and the two general expressions that explain it

examples.title: The one temperature that reads the same on both scales
examples.body:
Celsius to Fahrenheit is $f(x) = 1.8x + 32$, and going back is its inverse, $f^{-1}(x) = \tfrac{x - 32}{1.8}$. Every pair you know sits on it: 32°F for freezing, 212°F for boiling.

Now ask where the two scales agree — where $f(x) = x$. That is $1.8x + 32 = x$, so $0.8x = -32$ and $x = -40$. Minus forty degrees Celsius **is** minus forty degrees Fahrenheit, which is why the phrase is quoted without a unit.

It happens once and only once, and the reason is that both rules are straight lines: two lines that are not parallel cross exactly once. A function and its inverse always meet on the line $y = x$ if they meet at all, and here the crossing has a name people use.

visual.alt: The Celsius to Fahrenheit line crossing the line where the two scales are equal, at minus forty on both axes, the single point where a temperature reads the same in either scale

examples.title: Rounding cannot be undone
examples.body:
£4.51, £5.00 and £5.49 all round to £5. Three inputs, one output — which is allowed, because a function only promises one output per input, not one input per output.

What is lost is the way back. Handed £5 you cannot say which it came from, so rounding has no inverse, and no amount of cleverness supplies one. The most any line can be out by is 49p, in either direction.

That is the test for an inverse, and it is worth carrying: a function can be undone exactly when no two inputs share an output. Squaring fails it, because 3 and −3 both give 9 — which is why $\sqrt{\ }$ is defined as the positive root and why a square-rooted equation needs both signs putting back by hand.

visual.alt: A table of three different amounts that all round to the same five pounds, with the return journey unanswerable, which is what it means for a function to have no inverse

steps.title: A function is a machine
steps.body:
A **function** takes a number in, does something to it, and gives a number out. The notation is a way of naming that machine.

$$f(x) = 3x - 2$$

reads as: the function called $f$ takes an input, multiplies it by $3$, then subtracts $2$.

> $f(3)$ does **not** mean $f \times 3$.

It means **put $3$ in wherever $x$ appears**. So $f(3) = 3 \times 3 - 2 = 7$, and $f(4) = 3 \times 4 - 2 = 10$.

**Negatives need brackets.** For $f(x) = 3x - 2$, $f(-2) = 3 \times (-2) - 2 = -6 - 2 = -8$. Write the bracket in; it costs nothing and it prevents a sign error.

**A different kind of question.** $f(x) = 13$ does not ask you to substitute anything — it gives you the **output** and asks for the **input**. That makes it an equation:

$$3x - 2 = 13, \quad 3x = 15, \quad x = 5.$$

So the two look alike and ask opposite things. $f(5)$ asks "what comes out when $5$ goes in?" and $f(x) = 13$ asks "what went in to give $13$?"

steps.title: Composite functions: the inner one goes first
steps.body:
Two machines can be joined so the output of one becomes the input of the next. That is a **composite function**, and it is written by putting the two letters together.

$$fg(x) \text{ means } f(g(x)).$$

> Read it from the **inside out**. $g$ acts on $x$ first, and then $f$ acts on whatever $g$ produced.

That feels backwards, because $f$ is written first but happens second. It is the single most common error in this topic, and the cure is to rewrite $fg(x)$ as $f(g(x))$ before doing anything at all.

With $f(x) = 3x - 2$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 1$:

$$fg(2) = f(g(2)) = f(2^2 + 1) = f(5) = 3 \times 5 - 2 = 13.$$

Now the other way round:

$$gf(2) = g(f(2)) = g(3 \times 2 - 2) = g(4) = 4^2 + 1 = 17.$$

**Different answers from the same two functions and the same input.** That is the normal situation: $fg$ and $gf$ are different functions, and a question asking for both is expecting two different answers.

steps.title: Inverse functions: running the machine backwards
steps.body:
The **inverse** of $f$ undoes it. If $f$ turns $5$ into $13$, then $f^{-1}$ turns $13$ back into $5$.

> $f^{-1}(x)$ is the **inverse function**. It does not mean $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$.

To find it, rearrange in three steps.

1. Write $y = f(x)$.
2. **Swap** $x$ and $y$.
3. Make $y$ the subject.

For $f(x) = 3x - 2$:

$$y = 3x - 2 \quad \to \quad x = 3y - 2 \quad \to \quad x + 2 = 3y \quad \to \quad y = \frac{x + 2}{3}$$

So $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x + 2}{3}$. Write it in that form, not as $y = \ldots$.

**Now check it**, which takes seconds. $f(5) = 13$, and $f^{-1}(13) = \dfrac{13 + 2}{3} = \dfrac{15}{3} = 5$. Back where we started, so the inverse is right.

**Think of it as undoing the machine in reverse order.** $f$ multiplies by $3$ and then subtracts $2$. To undo that you add $2$ **first**, then divide by $3$ — the opposite operations, in the opposite order. That is exactly what $\dfrac{x + 2}{3}$ says.

visuals.alt: A function machine for the inverse, showing the input passing through an add two step and then a divide by three step, the opposite operations in the opposite order
A table of four functions with their inverses and a numerical check for each showing the inverse returns the original input

check.prompt: For $p(x) = 2x + 7$, find $p^{-1}(x)$. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
check.solution: Write $y = 2x + 7$, swap to get $x = 2y + 7$, then rearrange: $x - 7 = 2y$, so $y = \dfrac{x - 7}{2}$. Therefore $p^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x - 7}{2}$. Check: $p(4) = 15$ and $p^{-1}(15) = \tfrac{8}{2} = 4$.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
Throughout, $f(x) = 3x - 2$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 1$.

**Part A — substituting.**

1. Work out $f(4)$.
2. Work out $g(-4)$.
3. Solve $f(x) = 13$.

**Part B — composites.**

4. Work out $fg(2)$ and $gf(2)$, and say why they are different.
5. Find $fg(x)$ as a simplified expression.
6. Find $gf(x)$ as a simplified expression.

**Part C — inverses.**

7. Find $f^{-1}(x)$, and check it by running $5$ through $f$ and the answer back through $f^{-1}$.
8. Solve $fg(x) = 49$.

For question 6, keep the bracket round $3x - 2$ until you expand the square. The middle term is the one that disappears if you do not.

steps.title: Going deeper: composites in equations, and a function that is its own inverse
steps.body:
**Solving a composite equation.** Once you have $fg(x)$ as an expression, an equation in it is an ordinary equation.

With $fg(x) = 3x^2 + 1$, solve $fg(x) = 49$:

$$3x^2 + 1 = 49, \quad 3x^2 = 48, \quad x^2 = 16, \quad x = \pm 4.$$

**Two answers, and both count.** A squared term almost always produces a pair, and dropping the negative is a lost mark. Check: $g(-4) = 17$ and $f(17) = 49$. It works.

**Where $f$ and its inverse agree.** Take $h(x) = 2x - 7$. Rearranging gives $h^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x + 7}{2}$.

Now solve $h(x) = h^{-1}(x)$:

$$2x - 7 = \frac{x + 7}{2}$$
$$4x - 14 = x + 7$$
$$3x = 21, \quad x = 7.$$

Check both sides: $h(7) = 14 - 7 = 7$, and $h^{-1}(7) = \dfrac{14}{2} = 7$. They agree, and the value is the one that $h$ leaves unchanged.

**One more piece of notation.** $ff^{-1}(x) = x$ for **every** $x$, because doing a thing and then undoing it changes nothing. So $ff^{-1}(7) = 7$ without any calculation at all, whatever $f$ happens to be. A question that looks like it needs three lines of work sometimes needs none.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- $f(x)$ names a machine. $f(3)$ means **put $3$ in wherever $x$ appears** — it is not $f \times 3$.
- Bracket a negative input before squaring it: $g(-4) = (-4)^2 + 1 = 17$.
- $f(x) = k$ is an **equation**: it gives the output and asks for the input.
- $fg(x)$ means $f(g(x))$, so **$g$ goes first**. Rewrite it inside out before you start.
- Keep the bracket round the inner function when you substitute it.
- $(3x - 2)^2 = 9x^2 - 12x + 4$. The middle term is the one people lose.
- $fg(x)$ and $gf(x)$ are **different functions**. Expect different answers.
- $f^{-1}(x)$ is the **inverse**, not $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$.
- To find it: $y = f(x)$, swap $x$ and $y$, make $y$ the subject.
- An inverse undoes the operations in the **opposite order**, each replaced by its opposite.
- Check an inverse by running a number through both ways.
- $ff^{-1}(x) = x$ always, so questions like $ff^{-1}(7)$ need no working.
- Write the answer as $f^{-1}(x) = \ldots$, not as $y = \ldots$.

questions.solution: $f(-2) = 3 \times (-2) - 2 = -6 - 2 = -8$. Bracketing the negative before multiplying is what keeps the signs straight.
The bracket holds the **input** to the function, so $f(5)$ means put $5$ in wherever $x$ appears in the rule for $f$. It is never a multiplication.
This gives the output and asks for the input, so solve $3x - 2 = 13$. Adding $2$ gives $3x = 15$, so $x = 5$. Check: $f(5) = 15 - 2 = 13$.
$fg(2) = f(g(2))$, so $g$ acts first: $g(2) = 2^2 + 1 = 5$. Then $f(5) = 3 \times 5 - 2 = 13$. Doing them the other way round gives $17$, which is a different question.

questions.prompt: Which function acts on $x$ first in the composite $gf(x)$?
options: It depends on the value of $x$
questions.solution: $gf(x)$ is shorthand for $g(f(x))$, and the inner bracket is worked out first. So $f$ acts on $x$ and $g$ acts on the result — the function written second happens first.
$mn(x) = m(n(x)) = m(x + 3) = 4(x + 3) - 1 = 4x + 12 - 1 = 4x + 11$. The answer $4x + 2$ is $nm(x)$, the other order.

questions.prompt: For $p(x) = 2x + 7$, find $p^{-1}(x)$. Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
questions.solution: Write $y = 2x + 7$, swap the letters to get $x = 2y + 7$, then rearrange: $x - 7 = 2y$, so $y = \dfrac{x - 7}{2}$. Hence $p^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x - 7}{2}$.

Swap and rearrange: $x = 3y - 2$, so $x + 2 = 3y$ and $y = \dfrac{x + 2}{3}$. Check: $f(5) = 13$ and $\dfrac{13 + 2}{3} = 5$. $\dfrac{1}{3x - 2}$ is $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$, which is a different thing entirely.
$fg(x) = f(g(x)) = f(x^2 + 1) = 3(x^2 + 1) - 2 = 3x^2 + 3 - 2 = 3x^2 + 1$. The answer $9x^2 - 12x + 5$ is $gf(x)$, the other order.

questions.prompt: For $f(x) = 3x - 2$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 1$, find $gf(x)$, giving your answer in its simplest form.
questions.solution: $gf(x) = g(f(x)) = g(3x - 2) = (3x - 2)^2 + 1$. Expanding the square gives $9x^2 - 12x + 4$, and adding the $1$ gives $9x^2 - 12x + 5$. The middle term $-12x$ is the one that disappears if the bracket is dropped.

questions.prompt: For $m(x) = 4x - 1$ and $n(x) = x + 3$, which statement is true?
questions.solution: $mn(x) = m(x + 3) = 4(x + 3) - 1 = 4x + 11$, while $nm(x) = n(4x - 1) = 4x - 1 + 3 = 4x + 2$. They are different functions, which is the normal situation.

questions.prompt: A function $f$ has an inverse $f^{-1}$. What is $ff^{-1}(7)$?
options: It cannot be found without knowing $f$
questions.solution: The inverse undoes the function, so applying one after the other leaves the input unchanged. $ff^{-1}(x) = x$ for every $x$ and every $f$, so the answer is $7$ with no calculation at all.

questions.prompt: For $f(x) = 3x - 2$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 1$, $fg(x) = 3x^2 + 1$. Solve $fg(x) = 49$, giving the positive value of $x$.
questions.solution: Set $3x^2 + 1 = 49$, so $3x^2 = 48$ and $x^2 = 16$. That gives $x = 4$ or $x = -4$, and the question asks for the positive one, so $x = 4$. Check: $g(4) = 17$ and $f(17) = 49$.

Cubing is undone by taking the cube root, so $q^{-1}(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}$. Check: $q(2) = 8$ and $\sqrt[3]{8} = 2$. The option $\dfrac{1}{x^3}$ is the reciprocal, which is what $f^{-1}$ does **not** mean.

questions.prompt:
$f(x) = 3x - 2$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 1$.

(a) Find $fg(x)$, giving your answer in its simplest form.

(b) Find $gf(x)$, giving your answer in its simplest form.

(c) Solve $fg(x) = 49$.
questions.solution: For part a, f g of x means f of g of x, so g acts first. That gives f of, bracket, x squared plus one. Now substitute the whole of that bracket into f, which multiplies its input by three and subtracts two: three times, bracket, x squared plus one, bracket, minus two. Expanding gives three x squared plus three minus two, which simplifies to three x squared plus one. For part b, g f of x means g of f of x, so this time f acts first, giving g of, bracket, three x minus two. The function g squares its input and adds one, so this is, bracket, three x minus two, bracket, squared, plus one. Expanding the square gives nine x squared minus twelve x plus four; the middle term of minus twelve x comes from two lots of three x times minus two, and it is the term most often lost. Adding the one gives nine x squared minus twelve x plus five. Notice this is completely different from the answer to part a, which is normal. For part c, use the answer to part a. Setting three x squared plus one equal to forty nine and subtracting one gives three x squared equals forty eight, so x squared equals sixteen. Taking the square root gives x equals four or x equals minus four, and both are solutions because both square to sixteen.

questions.prompt:
$h(x) = 2x - 7$.

(a) Find $h^{-1}(x)$.

(b) Verify your answer by showing that $h^{-1}(h(6)) = 6$.

(c) Solve $h(x) = h^{-1}(x)$.
questions.solution: For part a, start by writing y equals two x minus seven. Swap the letters so it reads x equals two y minus seven, then make y the subject. Adding seven to both sides gives x plus seven equals two y, and dividing by two gives y equals x plus seven, all over two. So h inverse of x is x plus seven over two. It helps to see why: h multiplies by two and then subtracts seven, so the inverse adds seven first and then divides by two, the opposite operations in the opposite order. For part b, work out h of six first. Two times six is twelve, minus seven is five, so h of six is five. Now put five into the inverse: five plus seven is twelve, and twelve over two is six. That returns the original input of six, which confirms the inverse is correct. For part c, set the two expressions equal to each other: two x minus seven equals x plus seven, all over two. Multiply every term by two to clear the fraction, giving four x minus fourteen equals x plus seven. Subtracting x from both sides gives three x minus fourteen equals seven, and adding fourteen gives three x equals twenty one, so x equals seven. Checking, h of seven is fourteen minus seven, which is seven, and h inverse of seven is fourteen over two, which is also seven, so the two functions do agree there.

examTechnique.body:
**Substitute carefully, and bracket the negatives.** For $f(x) = x^2 - 3x$, $f(-2)$ is $(-2)^2 - 3(-2) = 4 + 6 = 10$. Without the brackets it is easy to produce $-4 - 6$.

**$f(x) = k$ is an equation to solve**, not a substitution. It gives you the output and asks for the input, so set the expression equal to $k$ and solve for $x$.

**$fg(x)$ means do $g$ first.** Write $f(g(x))$ out in full before you touch anything. Substitute the whole of $g(x)$ into $f$, brackets and all.

**$fg(x)$ and $gf(x)$ are almost never the same.** If a question asks for both, expect different answers — getting the same one twice usually means the order was applied the same way both times.

**For an inverse, rearrange.** $y = f(x)$, swap to $x = f(y)$, make $y$ the subject. Finish by writing the answer as $f^{-1}(x) = \ldots$, not as $y = \ldots$.

**Check your inverse.** Run a number through $f$ and then through $f^{-1}$. If it comes back, the inverse is right.

**Watch the notation.** $f^{-1}(x)$ means the inverse function. It does **not** mean $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$.
examinerErrors: Losing a bracket in $g(f(x))$, so $(3x - 2)^2$ becomes $3x^2 - 2$ or $9x^2 + 4$.
Squaring $(3x - 2)$ as $9x^2 + 4$, forgetting the middle term $-12x$.
Leaving the inverse written as $y = \ldots$ rather than $f^{-1}(x) = \ldots$.
Substituting into $f(x) = k$ instead of solving it.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer writes the composite out as f of g of x before substituting anything, and keeps the bracket round the inner function all the way through the expansion, so the middle term of a square is never lost. It finds an inverse by rearranging rather than by guessing, states the result in the f to the minus one of x form, and then checks it by running a number through both ways. It knows that f g of x and g f of x are different functions and does not expect them to agree, and it never reads f to the minus one as a reciprocal.
